u N)$. Choose a root coordinate $\alpha$ with $s\alpha=-\alpha$. Since $R=R^s\oplus\alpha R^s$, the coefficient-of-$\alpha$ map $\ell:R	o R^s$ has pairing matrix $ egin{pmatrix}0&1\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ on $1,\alpha$, hence identifies $R$ with its $R^s$-dual. Extending the right parameter identifies $\operatorname{Hom}_{A^s}(A,-)$ with $A\otimes_{A^s}-$, including the left $A$ action. Consequently $V_R	heta_s\cong A\otimes_{A^s}V_R\cong R\otimes_{R^s}V_R$ by actual action-compatible maps. This argument uses adjunction and relative Frobenius duality, not an isomorphism of residues.

For a polynomial Bott-Samelson bimodule $B$, $M=B\otimes_SR$ is finite free over the right $R$. A left denominator nonzero at the origin acts invertibly: modulo the right maximal ideal its constant plus positive-degree part is invertible, since positive left invariants annihilate the finite-dimensional coinvariant reduction and positive-degree operators there are nilpotent; Nakayama makes its matrix invertible over $R$. Both left and right actions therefore extend to $R$. Weyl invariants balance across every tensor factor, so these actions factor through $A$. Iterating the map in step 1.2 identifies the localized polynomial tensor word with $V_R$ of the deformed wall word, with empty word the identity graph $R=V_R\Delta_R(\lambda)$. All identifications preserve the generic tuple branches and the right parameter. The fixed average coordinate in the type-A permutation model is split off before this construction.

Let $Q,Q'$ be deformed block projectives. Their canonical comparison under $V_R$ is an isomorphism at every height-one prime. At nonroot primes, the distinct simple Verma components give one-label Morita equivalences; at root primes, each projective decomposes into the two elementary projectives of step 1.1 by lifting its actual residue decomposition with the projective Hom base-change maps in [F3], so that step verifies every pair of summands. The source Hom module is finite free over $R$ by [F3]. The target $\operatorname{Hom}_A(V_RQ,V_RQ')$ need not be assumed free in advance: it is the submodule of finite free $\operatorname{Hom}_R(V_RQ,V_RQ')$ satisfying the finitely many linear commutation equations for a finite $R$-basis of $A$. Inside the generic Hom space it is the intersection of its height-one localizations, since a rational matrix belongs to the free ambient matrix lattice precisely when all its height-one localizations do, and the $A$-linearity equations already hold generically. The coefficientwise UFD intersection argument of the central-action lemma gives the same intersection property for the source Hom lattice. Their height-one equalities therefore prove the comparison is an isomorphism over $R$; in particular the target is now free. This is full faithfulness on deformed projectives.

For polynomial Bott-Samelson modules $M,M'$ the module $\operatorname{Hom}_A(M,M')$ is the localization of the polynomial Hom module, and the composite $\operatorname{Hom}_A(M,M')\otimes_R\mathbb C\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O_R}(Q_R,Q_R')\otimes_R\mathbb C\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O}(Q,Q')\cong\operatorname{Hom}_C(VQ,VQ')$ is the natural reduction map by step 3.1, projective Hom base change and the ordinary Struktursatz, all maps being the canonical composition maps; hence reduction-of-Hom holds for Bott-Samelson modules and, by taking summands, for all polynomial Soergel bimodules, the degree components giving the graded statement.

Absolute complex extension follows by the actual same equations as real extension, not by a real-only assertion. For the rational $B_w$, write $E_{\mathbb Q}^0$ for its finite-dimensional local degree-zero endomorphism algebra and $J_{\mathbb Q}$ for its nilpotent radical; [F4] gives $E_{\mathbb Q}^0/J_{\mathbb Q}=\mathbb Q$. Fixed-degree maps are kernels of finite rational linear commutation equations on homogeneous generator images. Tensoring these equations with the flat field $\mathbb C$ identifies $E_{\mathbb C}^0=E_{\mathbb Q}^0\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C$. Its ideal $J_{\mathbb Q}\otimes\mathbb C$ is nilpotent and its quotient is $\mathbb C$, so every element with nonzero scalar residue is invertible by a finite geometric series; hence this is a local algebra with residue $\mathbb C$. The same flat equations preserve its top graph and degree. Extending each rational word decomposition gives a complex decomposition into these absolutely indecomposable labels; finite Krull--Schmidt uniqueness then classifies every summand of every complex word. Thus the normalized polynomial $B_w$ has the required local degree-zero algebra over $\mathbb C$. Step 4.1 makes the degree-zero algebra of $\bar B_w$ its quotient, hence local. Here is the needed passage to ungraded endomorphisms. For the finite-dimensional graded algebra $E=\operatorname{End}(\bar B_w)$, grading scalings preserve its Jacobson radical $J$; interpolation in finitely many distinct scaling parameters extracts every homogeneous component, so $J$ is graded. The semisimple quotient $E/J$ is a product of matrix algebras by [F6]. Its grading derivation preserves each factor, since a derivation kills central idempotents. Every derivation $D$ of $\operatorname{Mat}_n(\mathbb C)$ is inner: with matrix units, $H=\sum_i D(e_{i1})e_{1i}$ satisfies $D(a)=Ha-aH$, by applying the product rule to $e_{ij}e_{k1}$ and summing in $k$. The grading derivation is diagonalizable; writing $H=H_s+H_n$ shows $\operatorname{ad}H_n=0$, because it is the commuting nilpotent part of $\operatorname{ad}H$. A scalar nilpotent matrix is zero, so $H$ is semisimple up to an irrelevant scalar. Its degree-zero centralizer is consequently a product of matrix algebras on its eigenspaces. Thus $(E/J)_0$ is semisimple. It is a quotient of the local $E_0$, so it equals $\mathbb C$; a product of such centralizers can have dimension one only if there is a single matrix factor of size one. Hence $E/J=\mathbb C$, and $E$ is local. This proves that $\bar B_w$ remains indecomposable after forgetting grading; it supplies the graded-algebra argument rather than attributing innerness to Wedderburn-Artin.

The normalized top summand is self-dual without assuming an unproved indecomposable-form assertion. In the unshifted tensor ring of a length-$k$ word, each added reflection factor is a quadratic finite free extension with basis $1,\alpha_s$ and relation $\alpha_s^2\in S^s$. The coefficient-of-$\alpha_s$ functional has perfect pairing matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$; composing these functionals along the tensor tower gives a perfect right-$S$ pairing on its rank-$2^k$ basis. It is left-invariant by commutativity of the tensor ring. The total trace has degree $-2k$, so shifting the word by $(k)$ gives a degree-zero isomorphism from the Bott-Samelson bimodule to its invariant right dual $D B=\operatorname{Hom}_S(B,S)$. For a reduced word of $w$, $B_w$ is the unique summand with nonzero top graph $w$, of generic right rank one there; all other summands have strictly lower graph support by [F4]. Duality preserves generic graph branches: a left scalar on a rank-one branch acts by the same scalar on its right dual. Therefore $D B_w$ is an indecomposable summand of the very same self-dual word, has its $w$ branch, and must be the identical unique top summand, with no shift. Thus $B_w\cong D B_w$. Finite right projectivity makes duality commute with right origin reduction, so $\bar B_w$ has a graded self-duality centered at zero. Any two finite graded lifts with the same indecomposable underlying $C$-module differ by a shift: homogeneous components of an ungraded isomorphism and its inverse give $1=\sum_d g_{-d}f_d$ in the local degree-zero endomorphism algebra; one summand is a unit, so $f_d$ is an isomorphism after a shift (its source and target have the same finite dimension). A nonzero shift cannot preserve centered self-duality, by symmetry of the extreme degrees. This proves unique centered normalization; rank one has degrees $-1,1$, and an uncentered shift gives $0,2$.

Induction on Bruhat length gives the label dictionary: for a reduced word $w=s_1\cdots s_k$, $P(w\cdot\lambda)$ is the unique new top-label summand of $\theta_{s_k}\cdots\theta_{s_1}\Delta(\lambda)$ by [F2], and applying $V$ and the iterated wall-crossing formula gives the new summand of the reduced left tensor word $\overline{B_{s_k}\cdots B_{s_1}}$, whose top graph label is the inverse $w^{-1}$, while every proper subexpression contributes already-matched smaller labels; full faithfulness of step 3.1 for the deformed side and the indecomposability of step 5.1 match the two new summands uniquely, so $VP(w\cdot\lambda)\cong\bar B_{w^{-1}}$, and distinct labels remain non-isomorphic because $V$ is fully faithful on projectives.

The type-A equivalence and normalized dictionary follow from steps 4.1 through 6.2. For a semisimple product of type-A factors, reflection words reorder into the independent factor words and their reductions are tensor products of the factor reductions. Their endomorphism algebra is the tensor product of the finite factor endomorphism algebras: in finite bases, the commutation equations for the two independent coefficient algebras give this tensor-Hom identity. Each factor algebra is local with residue $\mathbb C$ by step 5.1; the sum of its tensor-extended radicals is nilpotent and its quotient is $\mathbb C$, so the product reduction is indecomposable. The labels, inverse convention and centered self-duality therefore combine factorwise; a rank-zero factor contributes the unit. The ungraded equivalence for every complex semisimple type needs no unprovided diagrammatic classification: define its Weyl-group Soergel-module category as the additive category of summands of polynomial Bott-Samelson right reductions. For every reflection realization, $S=S^s\oplus\alpha_sS^s$, and Weyl invariants balance across the tensor factors; the elementary quotient computation gives $B_s\otimes_SC=(C\otimes_{C^s}C)(1)$ exactly as in the wall-crossing theorem. Thus forgetting shifts identifies all right-reduced words with the ordinary $V$-images of wall words starting at $V\Delta(\lambda)=\mathbb C$. Ordinary full faithfulness [F1] lifts every idempotent between these images uniquely to an idempotent of their projective words. Since all projectives occur as summands of such words by [F2], this is a fully faithful and essentially surjective equivalence in every type. Its indecomposable labels can be read from the unique new projective summands themselves. The additional type-A polynomial/diagrammatic label and centered self-dual normalization are exactly those established in steps 5.1 through 6.2; no type-A classification is substituted for a general-type classification.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and work in a regular integral type-A block over
$\mathbb C$. With the page's right wall-crossing convention and left
$C$-module values of $V$, there is an equivalence
$$V\colon\operatorname{Proj}(\mathcal O_\lambda)\xrightarrow{\sim}\{\text{ungraded Soergel modules }B\otimes_S\mathbb C\},\qquad P(w\cdot\lambda)\longmapsto\bar B_{w^{-1}}.$$
The target is the additive category of direct summands of the right reductions
of polynomial Bott-Samelson bimodules, or equivalently of iterated
$C\otimes_{C^s}(-)$ applied to the trivial module $\mathbb C$, not to the
regular module $C$. For $w=s_1\cdots s_k$, the projective is the unique new
top-label summand of $\theta_{s_k}\cdots\theta_{s_1}\Delta(\lambda)$; applying
$V$ gives the new summand of $\overline{B_{s_k}\cdots B_{s_1}}$, thus the
inverse label. These normalized indecomposable polynomial lifts supply
self-dual auxiliary gradings; in rank one the centered degrees are $-1,1$,
with degrees $0,2$ after an uncentered shift. Forgetting grading recovers the
projective dictionary. More generally the ungraded equivalence with
Weyl-group Soergel modules holds for every complex semisimple regular integral
block; the type-A diagrammatic label comparison applies only in type A.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\lambda$ be dominant regular integral,
$R=S(\mathfrak h)_{(0)}$ the localization at the origin, and use the selected
component $\mathcal D_R^{[\lambda]}(\lambda)$ of the tensor-generated deformed
family of [[def-the-deformed-category-o-family-and-its-specializations]]. For
every $x\in W$ there is a projective $P_R(x,\lambda)$ in the deformed
$\lambda$-block whose residue fiber is $P(x\cdot\lambda)$; it is unique up to
isomorphism, and every indecomposable of this selected tensor component is one
of these lifts. Each lift has a finite deformed Verma flag with the same
multiplicities as its closed fiber. More generally, a finite projective in this
block is a direct summand of a finite sum of truncated induced projectives
representing relative weight spaces; for every map of deformation algebras
$R\to R'$ its base change is projective in the corresponding truncated category
and
$$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O_R}(P,N)\otimes_RR'\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O_{R'}}(P\otimes_RR',N\otimes_RR').$$
For a finite Verma-filtered target $N$ this Hom module is finite free over
local $R$. A $\mathfrak g\otimes R$-linear map between such finite
projective/Verma-filtered objects whose residue fiber is an isomorphism is
itself an isomorphism, weight by weight. For a dot-dominant integral target
$\nu$, including singular $\nu$, the same local projective construction gives
all lifts in its deformed block, with labels the distinct cosets $W/W_\nu$;
these lifts belong to the target component $\mathcal D_R^{[\nu]}(\lambda)$ of a
regular-source tensor family. It is neither necessary nor asserted that the
singular Verma itself generates every target projective, and the other central
components of the full tensor family are not claimed to have only these
indecomposables.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\lambda$ be dominant regular integral,
$S=S(\mathfrak h)$, $R=S_{(0)}$, and $P_R=P_R(w_0,\lambda)$ the deformed
antidominant projective. Write $\operatorname{HC}_\rho\colon Z(U(\mathfrak g))\to S^W$
for the published shifted Harish-Chandra isomorphism,
$\sigma_\lambda(f)(\epsilon)=f(\lambda+\rho+\epsilon)$, and define
$$a_\lambda\colon Z\otimes_{\mathbb C}R\longrightarrow R\otimes_{R^W}R,\qquad z\otimes r\longmapsto\sigma_\lambda(\operatorname{HC}_\rho(z))\otimes r.$$
Then $a_\lambda$ and the action map $Z\otimes R\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathfrak g\otimes R}(P_R)$
are surjective and have the same kernel, inducing a canonical $R$-algebra
isomorphism
$$\operatorname{End}_{\mathfrak g\otimes R}(P_R)\cong R\otimes_{R^W}R.$$
On a generic Verma constituent of highest weight $x\cdot\lambda+\epsilon$, $z$
acts by the scalar
$\operatorname{HC}_\rho(z)(x(\lambda+\rho)+\epsilon)=\sigma_\lambda(\operatorname{HC}_\rho(z))(x^{-1}\epsilon)$;
these scalars vary with $x$, and the center need not act by a single scalar on
$P_R$. After tensoring the right $R$ factor with the residue field at $0$, the
endomorphism algebra becomes $C=S/(S^W_+S)$. More generally, for dot-dominant
integral $\nu$ the corresponding algebra is $R^{W_\nu}\otimes_{R^W}R$, where
$W_\nu$ is the dot stabilizer. Translation out of that facet identifies the
singular antidominant projective with the regular one; under these shifted
Harish-Chandra identifications, its induced endomorphism map is the inclusion
$R^{W_\nu}\otimes_{R^W}R\hookrightarrow R\otimes_{R^W}R$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For a regular integral block and simple reflection
$s$, with $C=\operatorname{End}(P(w_0\cdot\lambda))$, there is a natural
isomorphism of functors to left $C$-modules
$$V\theta_s\cong C\otimes_{C^s}V.$$
Equivalently the functor is tensoring by the $(C,C)$-bimodule
$C\otimes_{C^s}C$, with left action on the first factor and right action on the
second. In type A over $\mathbb C$, its polynomial lift is tensoring on the
left by $B_s=S\otimes_{S^s}S(1)$; read up to the auxiliary suspension
normalisation fixed by the rank-one case, the right origin reduction of $B_s$
is the two-dimensional module of centered degrees $-1,1$, for $M=S$ the
coinvariant reduction satisfies
$B_s\otimes_SC\cong(C\otimes_{C^s}C)(1)$ in the same normalisation, and
$B_s\otimes_S\mathbb C$ itself is not the bimodule $C\otimes_{C^s}C$: the
former has vector-space dimension two, whereas the latter has dimension
$2|W|$. Forgetting the grading gives the displayed category-$\mathcal O$
formula, and no grading on arbitrary category-$\mathcal O$ objects is asserted.

**Graphs and supports.** Keep $k=\mathbb Q$, $R=\mathbb Q[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ with
$\deg x_i=2$, and the affine scheme $V=\mathbb A^n_k=\operatorname{Spec}R$,
whose $k$-points are $V(k)=k^n$. Use the place-permuting action of $S_n$
from [[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]].
For $w\in S_n$ let
$$Gr(w):=\operatorname{Graph}(w:V\to V)\subseteq V\times_kV,\quad Gr(w)(k)=\{(w\lambda,\lambda):\lambda\in k^n\},\qquad Gr(A):=\bigcup_{w\in A}Gr(w)\ \ (A\subseteq S_n),$$
so that $V\times_kV=\operatorname{Spec}(R\otimes_kR)$ and $Gr(w)$ is the graph
of the map $\lambda\mapsto w\lambda$. A graded $(R,R)$-bimodule $M$ is the
same thing as a graded module over $R\otimes_kR$, and the support of $m\in M$ is
the zero set $\operatorname{supp}(m):=V(\operatorname{Ann}(m))\subseteq V\times V$
of its annihilator ideal in $R\otimes_kR$. For $A\subseteq S_n$ put
$$\Gamma_AM:=\{m\in M:\operatorname{supp}(m)\subseteq Gr(A)\},$$
a graded sub-bimodule of $M$. Since $Gr(A)$ is closed with radical ideal
$I(Gr(A))=\bigcap_{w\in A}I(Gr(w))$ (an intersection of prime ideals, since each
$Gr(w)$ is a linear subspace of $V\times V$ complementing the second factor), an
element $m$ lies in $\Gamma_AM$ exactly when $I(Gr(A))^N m=0$ for some $N\ge0$:
this is the Nullstellensatz together with the Noetherianity of
$R\otimes_kR$. The ideal itself need not annihilate such an element — in
$(R\otimes_kR)/I(Gr(e))^2$ the class of $1$ is supported on $Gr(e)$ but is not
killed by $I(Gr(e))$ — which is why the criterion is stated with a power of the
ideal. For $i\in\mathbb Z$ we write
$$\Gamma_{\ge i}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\ell(x)\ge i\}}M,\qquad \Gamma_{\le i}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\ell(x)\le i\}}M,$$
using the length function of [[lem-type-a-reduced-words-are-connected-by-braid-moves]],
while for $y\in S_n$ the $y$-indexed symbols denote the *Bruhat
principal-set* cutoffs of Soergel's Notation 6.1,
$$\Gamma_{\le y}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\,x\le y\}}M,\qquad \Gamma_{<y}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\,x<y\}}M,\qquad \Gamma_{\ge y}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\,x\ge y\}}M,\qquad \Gamma_{>y}M:=\Gamma_{\{x:\,x>y\}}M,$$
with $\Gamma_yM:=\Gamma_{\{y\}}M$ the elements concentrated on the single graph
$Gr(y)$ and $\Gamma_{\ne y}M:=\Gamma_{S_n\setminus\{y\}}M$ the elements
concentrated off $Gr(y)$. The integer-indexed symbols of the previous display are
the *length* cutoffs used to define the flags below, and they must not be
confused with the element-indexed Bruhat cutoffs: for $y=s_1$ in $S_4$ the
submodule $\Gamma_{\le1}M$ contains $Gr(s_3)$ while
$\Gamma_{\le y}M=\Gamma_{\{e,s_1\}}M$ does not, and the two cutoffs agree at
the extremes, $\Gamma_{\le w_0}=\Gamma_{\le\ell(w_0)}=M$ and
$\Gamma_{<e}=\Gamma_{\le-1}=0$. So
$\Gamma^yM:=M/\Gamma_{\ne y}M$ is Soergel's $y$-layer
*quotient*; following Soergel's
Notation 6.1 we write the two $y$-layer quotients with an underline,
$$\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M:=\Gamma_{\le y}M/\Gamma_{<y}M,\qquad \underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M:=\Gamma_{\ge y}M/\Gamma_{>y}M,$$
so that $\underline{\Gamma}_{\le y}M$ is the quotient of the lower support
submodule by $\Gamma_{<y}M$ and $\underline{\Gamma}_{\ge y}M$ the quotient of
the upper support submodule by the part supported strictly above $Gr(y)$.

**Standard bimodules.** For $w\in S_n$ let $R_w$ be the graded $(R,R)$-bimodule
which equals $R$ as a graded $k$-vector space and has
$$f\cdot x=fx,\qquad x\cdot g=w(g)\,x\qquad(f,g,x\in R),$$
where $w(g)(\lambda):=g(w^{-1}\lambda)$; $R_w$ is generated by the element $1$ of
degree $0$. Write $(k)$ for the *external* shift $M(k):=M\{-k\}$ of
[[def-graded-ring-module-bimodule-and-internal-shift]], so that
$M(k)_d=M_{d+k}$; this is the shift convention of the type-A sources, and it is
the one in which $B_i=R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R(1)$ of
[[def-type-a-soergel-bimodule-for-a-simple-reflection]] has $1\otimes1$ of
degree $-1$. Put
$$\Delta_w(d):=R_w(d-\ell(w)),\qquad \nabla_w(d):=R_w(d+\ell(w))\qquad(d\in\mathbb Z),$$
so that $\Delta_w(d)$ is the standard bimodule $R_w$ with its generator in
degree $\ell(w)-d$, and $\nabla_w(d)$ is $R_w$ with its generator in degree
$-\ell(w)-d$. Thus $\Delta_w(0)=R_w\{\ell(w)\}$,
$\nabla_w(0)=R_w\{-\ell(w)\}$ and $\Delta_e(d)=\nabla_e(d)=R(d)$ is generated
in degree $-d$; in particular $\Delta_e(0)=\nabla_e(0)=R_e=R$.

For graded free $R$-modules in this type-A page, a homogeneous free generator of degree $a$ contributes $v^a$ to graded rank. This is the $v\mapsto v^{-1}$ transform of Soergel's rank convention in his Notation 5.2; all rank formulas below use this convention.

**Support filtrations.** A $\Delta$-flag of a graded $R$-bimodule $M$ is a
finite chain $0=M_0\subseteq M_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq M_k=M$ of graded
sub-bimodules which refines the length filtration
$$M=\Gamma_{\ge0}M\supseteq\Gamma_{\ge1}M\supseteq\cdots\supseteq\Gamma_{\ge\ell(w_0)+1}M=0$$
of $M$ (here $\Gamma_{\ge0}M=M$ for every bimodule supported on
$Gr(S_n)=\bigcup_{w}Gr(w)$, which all bimodules of this page are, and
$\Gamma_{\ge i}M=0$ for $i>\ell(w_0)$ because no graph $Gr(x)$ with
$\ell(x)>i$ remains) and whose successive quotients are
standard bimodules $M_j/M_{j-1}\cong R_{x_j}\{a_j\}$. We require each
length layer to be a finite direct sum of shifted graph bimodules of that
length, as in Soergel's Definition 5.4. Thus the
quotients carry a numbering with $\ell(x_1)\ge\cdots\ge\ell(x_k)$ and each
$R_{x_j}\{a_j\}$ is one graph, so that $M$ has a "support flag" in the sense of
Soergel's $F_\Delta$. A $\nabla$-flag has the same direct-sum condition on its length layers, with the reverse length
filtration $\Gamma_{\le i}M$ and $\ell(x_1)\le\cdots\le\ell(x_k)$. The
refinement condition is a condition on supports, not an ordering of incomparable
quotients of equal length; only the lengths are ordered. For $i=\ell(x)$ the
graded multiplicity is
$$(M:\Delta_x(d)):=\text{multiplicity of }\Delta_x(d)\text{ in } \Gamma_{\ge i}M/\Gamma_{\ge i+1}M,$$
and, for a $\nabla$-flag, $(M:\nabla_x(d))$ is the multiplicity of
$\nabla_x(d)$ in $\Gamma_{\le i}M/\Gamma_{\le i-1}M$; a priori both symbols
refer to a chosen compatible enumeration (the next items on this page prove that
they do not depend on it). With $T_x$ the Hecke basis of
[[lem-type-a-hecke-standard-basis-for-soergel-comparison]] and
$\widetilde T_x:=v^{\ell(x)}T_x$, the character sums attached to a flag are
$$h_\Delta(M):=\sum_{x,d}(M:\Delta_x(d))\,v^d\,\widetilde T_x,\qquad h_\nabla(M):=\sum_{x,d}(M:\nabla_x(d))\,v^{-d}\,\widetilde T_x,$$
and they are used only through the items that prove these sums intrinsic.

**Small $n$.** For $n\le1$ there is a single element $e$ and every object is a finite direct sum of shifts $\bigoplus_j R(d_j)$. Its one-graph flags have these summands as quotients, so $h_\Delta=\sum_jv^{d_j}\widetilde T_e$ and $h_\nabla=\sum_jv^{-d_j}\widetilde T_e$; in particular both characters send the unit $R$ to $1$.

**The reduction.** Work over the ring $S=\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ of the real
scalar-extension definition ([[def-real-type-a-soergel-category-and-scalar-extension]]),
with $S_+=\bigoplus_{d>0}S_d$ the ideal of positive-degree elements; the residue
field of the right action is
$$k:=S/S_+=\mathbb R,$$
with quotient map $S\twoheadrightarrow k$, $s\mapsto \bar s$. For a graded
$(S,S)$-bimodule $M$ that is finite free as a right $S$-module put
$$\overline M:=M\otimes_Sk=M/MS_+,$$
the **reduction** of $M$: a finite-dimensional graded $k$-vector space, on which
the left $S$-action descends because $S_+\subseteq S$ is central and $MS_+$ is
stable under left multiplication. Write $\overline M^{\,i}$ for its homogeneous
component of degree $i$, $d_i(M):=\dim_{\mathbb R}\overline M^{\,i}$ for the
graded dimensions, and
$$\dim\overline M:=\sum_{i\in\mathbb Z}d_i(M)\,v^{-i}$$
for the **graded dimension** (a finite Laurent polynomial); all tensor products
below are over $S$. For a morphism $f:M\to M'$ of graded bimodules, i.e. a
degree-zero bi-$S$-linear map, the induced map
$$\overline f:\overline M\to\overline{M'},\qquad \overline f(m+MS_+):=f(m)+M'S_+ ,$$
is well defined and $k$-linear of degree zero, because $f(MS_+)\subseteq M'S_+$.
Reduction is a functor from finite right-free graded bimodules to finite
dimensional graded $k$-vector spaces; it preserves finite direct sums and
shifts, in the sense $\overline{M(d)}=\overline M(d)$ in the Elias-Williamson
shift convention $M(d)_e=M_{d+e}$.

**The dominant Lefschetz operator.** Fix a strictly dominant degree-two
element
$$\rho=\sum_{j=1}^nc_jx_j\in S_2,\qquad c_1>c_2>\cdots>c_n ,$$
which exists by [[def-real-type-a-soergel-category-and-scalar-extension]] (for
example $c_j=(n+1)/2-j$); recall that this is exactly the condition
$\rho(\alpha_i^\vee)>0$ for every simple coroot $\alpha_i^\vee$ in the
coordinate normalization of this page
([[def-finite-weyl-root-system-lattice-and-chamber-conventions]]). Let
$\rho\cdot(-):M\to M$, $m\mapsto\rho m$, denote left multiplication by $\rho$.
Since $S_+\subseteq S$ is central and $\rho\,(MS_+)\subseteq MS_+$, this
operator preserves the submodule $MS_+$ and therefore descends to a degree-two
$k$-linear endomorphism
$$L_0:=\rho\cdot(-):\overline M\longrightarrow\overline M,\qquad m+MS_+\longmapsto \rho m+MS_+,$$
called the **dominant Lefschetz operator** on $\overline M$. For rational
objects $B_x,B_s$ with real scalar extensions
$B_x^R=B_x\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb R$ and $B_s^R$, the same construction
applies to the reduced tensor product
$\overline{B_x^RB_s^R}=\overline{(B_xB_s)^R}$, where $B_xB_s$ denotes the
tensor product over the rational polynomial ring; the operator $L_0$ on it is
the value $\zeta=0$ of the deformed operator $L_\zeta$ defined later on this
page.

**Descent detection.** For every $w\in S_n$ and every simple reflection $s_i$
one has
$$(w\rho)(\alpha_i^\vee)>0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \ell(s_iw)>\ell(w).$$
Indeed, $(w\rho)(\alpha_i^\vee)=c_{w^{-1}(i)}-c_{w^{-1}(i+1)}$ is positive
exactly when $w^{-1}(i)<w^{-1}(i+1)$, the left-ascent criterion for inversion
length. Thus the displayed evaluation detects left descents; applied to
$w=x^{-1}$ it detects right descents of $x$, because $\ell(s_ix^{-1})=\ell(xs_i)$.

**Grading conventions.** The reduced module $\overline{B_x^R}$ has bottom degree
$-\ell(x)$ and top degree $+\ell(x)$; the unreduced bimodule has nonzero
components in arbitrarily high degrees. On a reduced module the "centered" degree $-i$ is the
internal degree $-i$, and the Lefschetz operator raises internal degree by two.
All homological (complex) shifts are written $[\,j\,]$ and all internal shifts
$(d)$, as on the rest of this page; the Bruhat order used throughout is the
rank-inequality order of
[[def-bruhat-order-on-the-symmetric-group]].

Let $B_w$ be the rational indecomposable type-A Soergel bimodule and let $B_w^R$ be its real scalar extension. (1) $B_w^R$ is indecomposable; its finite-dimensional degree-zero endomorphism algebra is local with residue field $\mathbb R$. If $S(w)$ holds, its degree-zero endomorphism algebra is $\mathbb R$, but no rank-one assertion for the full graded endomorphism module is made. (2) Real extension preserves the labels and shifts of all finite Krull-Schmidt decompositions of rational Soergel bimodules, and every real indecomposable is a unique $B_w^R(d)$. (3) $\Delta$/$\nabla$ support-filtration multiplicities, characters, reduction by positive-degree right polynomials, and Hom spaces commute with scalar extension; thus character identities over $\mathbb R$ descend to $\mathbb Q$. (4) If $xs>x$ and $S(y)$ holds for all $y<xs$, then $B_xB_s=B_{xs}\oplus\bigoplus_{y<xs}B_y^{a_y}$ with $a_y$ nonnegative integers and no grading shifts; the top summand occurs once. If $xs<x$ and $S(x)$ holds, then $B_xB_s=B_x(1)\oplus B_x(-1)$. All assertions concern the normalized self-dual indecomposables.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Every projective object
of $\mathcal O$ has a finite Verma flag
([[def-verma-flag-and-its-multiplicities]]).

More precisely, each projective cover $P(\mu)$ produced by
[[thm-category-o-has-enough-projectives]] is a direct summand of the
projective object $\operatorname{pr}_C(E\otimes M(\lambda))$ of
[[lem-finite-dimensional-tensors-reach-every-block-simple]], which is a
direct summand of $E\otimes M(\lambda)$; a general projective object has
finite length, hence is a finite direct sum of indecomposable projectives,
each of which is a projective cover of its simple head.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). For all weights
$\lambda$ and $\mu$,
$$(P(\lambda):\Delta(\mu))=[\Delta(\mu):L(\lambda)]=[M(\mu):L(\lambda)],$$
where $P(\lambda)$ is the projective cover of $L(\lambda)$, the left-hand
multiplicity is the Verma-flag multiplicity of
[[thm-projectives-in-category-o-have-verma-flags]], and the right-hand
multiplicity is the simple composition multiplicity of the Verma module
$M(\mu)$ ([[def-standard-and-costandard-objects-in-category-o]]).

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Work in category
$\mathcal O$ with the conventions of [[def-bgg-category-o]], and write
$\Delta(\mu)=M(\mu)$ for the standard objects of
[[def-standard-and-costandard-objects-in-category-o]], i.e. the Verma modules
of [[def-verma-module]].

A **finite Verma flag** of an object $X$ of $\mathcal O$ — also called a
**standard flag** or a **$\Delta$-flag** — is a finite increasing sequence of
subobjects
$$0=X_0\subseteq X_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq X_n=X$$
such that each quotient $X_i/X_{i-1}$ is isomorphic to a Verma module
$\Delta(\mu_i)=M(\mu_i)$, for $i=1,\dots,n$. An object admitting such a flag is
called **Verma-filtered**. Since the flag is exhausted by its factors, its
class in the Grothendieck group
$K_0(\mathcal O)$ of [[def-grothendieck-group-and-character-of-category-o]]
is
$$[X]=\sum_{i=1}^n[\Delta(\mu_i)].$$

For a Verma-filtered object $X$ and a weight $\mu$, the **multiplicity**
$(X:\Delta(\mu))$ is the number of indices $i$ with $\mu_i=\mu$ in a Verma
flag of $X$. This number is independent of the chosen flag by
[[lem-verma-flag-multiplicities-are-independent-of-the-flag]], so the notation
$(X:\Delta(\mu))$ is well-defined for Verma-filtered $X$.

The zero object has the empty flag, and every multiplicity of the zero object
is zero; a nonzero Verma-filtered object has at least one factor. A one-step
flag of $X$ is exactly an isomorphism $X\cong\Delta(\mu)$ for a single weight
$\mu$, so the objects with a one-step flag are the Verma modules themselves.
The flag is a chain of subobjects of $X$ in the module category; it is not
required to split, and later examples show that it need not.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be finite-dimensional complex
semisimple, $\lambda$ the dominant regular integral representative of a block
and $\mathcal O_\lambda$ its block with antidominant weight $w_0\cdot\lambda$.
Let $C$ be the coinvariant algebra of
[[def-the-coinvariant-algebra-of-a-finite-weyl-group]] for the Cartan
reflection representation, with its grading fixed there. Then:

(1) the natural maps $Z(U(\mathfrak g))\to C$ (Harish-Chandra isomorphism,
shifted by $\lambda+\rho$ in the published $\operatorname{HC}_\rho$ convention,
followed by the quotient map $\rho$) and $Z(U(\mathfrak g))\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathfrak g}P(w_0\cdot\lambda)$
(multiplication) are surjective with the same kernel;

(2) consequently the multiplication map induces a canonical algebra isomorphism
$$\operatorname{End}_{\mathfrak g}P(w_0\cdot\lambda)\ \cong\ C,$$
identifying $C$ with the endomorphism ring of the antidominant projective,
canonically and independently of the choice of projective cover inside its
isomorphism class;

(3) the grading on the right-hand side is the internal grading of the
coinvariant algebra; no graded lift of category $\mathcal O$ is asserted or
used.

This is Soergel's Endomorphismensatz [Soe90, Theorem 7], in the regular integral
case; the companion general form for singular blocks replaces $C$ by the
invariants $C^{W_\lambda}$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathcal O_\lambda$ be a regular integral block
with antidominant projective $P=P(w_0\cdot\lambda)$ and Soergel functor
$V=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O}(P,-)$, and let $C$ be the coinvariant
algebra, identified with $\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal O}(P)$ by
[[thm-endomorphisms-of-the-antidominant-projective-are-the-coinvariant-algebra]],
so that $V$ takes values in $C$-modules. Then for every $M\in\mathcal O_\lambda$
and every projective $Q\in\mathcal O_\lambda$ the canonical map
$$V\colon \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O_\lambda}(M,Q)\longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}_{C\text{-mod}}(VM,VQ)$$
is an isomorphism. In particular $V$ is fully faithful on the full subcategory
of projective objects of the block, and it is faithful on all of
$\mathcal O_\lambda$ after passing to the quotient by the Serre subcategory of
objects killed by $V$.

derivations.claim: The functor $V_R$ is exact and sends each deformed standard $\Delta_R(y\cdot\lambda)$ to a finite free $R$-module of rank one: by [F4] its closed fiber is one-dimensional, and by [F2] the Hom module into the Verma-filtered standard is finite free with base change, so the rank is one.

On that rank-one free module the center acts on the generic constituent of highest weight $y\cdot\lambda+\tau$ by the scalar $\operatorname{HC}_\rho(z)(y(\lambda+\rho)+\tau)=\sigma_\lambda(\operatorname{HC}_\rho(z))(y^{-1}\tau)$, which in the polynomial graph convention [F3] is the branch of the graph label $x=y^{-1}$; hence the graph label of the standard constituent is the inverse of its highest-weight label.

The preceding dictionary proves the deformed, action-compatible wall isomorphism $V_R\theta_s\cong R\otimes_{R^s}V_R$ by adjunction, the translated central inclusion and the coefficient-of-$\alpha_s$ Frobenius pairing; it also proves deformed full faithfulness and the natural reduction-of-Hom map. Iteration identifies the localized polynomial word with the $V_R$-image of its lifted projective word. The unique top-label polynomial summand and the top projective summand match under this full faithfulness, by the dictionary's length induction. Restriction to their matching idempotents therefore gives an actual $A$-module isomorphism $\mathsf B(P)\otimes_SR\cong V_RP_R$, preserving every generic branch. It is not inferred from a mere origin isomorphism.

Passing to the fraction field, the graph-support ranks of $\mathsf B(P)$ at $x$ are therefore the multiplicities of the deformed Verma constituents of $P_R$ at the inverse label $y=x^{-1}$, and flat localization preserves these ranks; the deformed Verma flag of $P_R$ specializes exactly to the Verma flag of $P$ by [F2], so summing the graded multiplicities gives $(P:\Delta(y\cdot\lambda))=\sum_dr_{y^{-1},d}(\mathsf B(P))$, which is the stated comparison at $v=1$.

These are ranks before origin reduction, so no intrinsic separated support filtration on $V(P)$ is asserted. For another complex semisimple type use the deformed lift $V_RP_R$ and its generic branch ranks, constructed in the preceding dictionary without type-A diagrammatic classification. Steps 1.1--1.2 identify each standard with its rank-one inverse branch in any reflection realization, so the same equality holds for these Weyl-group deformed lifts; whenever a corresponding polynomial lift is chosen, its localization has those same ranks. The type-A polynomial support-filtration formula is the particular case of step 2.1, with the fixed average coordinate split off.
